articles.title: Household paint and finish records
articles.summary: Keep an accurate record of decorative finishes without guessing at product compatibility.

sections.title: Record existing finishes
paragraphs: For each room, record the surface, colour name or product code if verified, and the location of retained labels or receipts. Photos may assist but lighting changes colour appearance.
Mark uncertain product names clearly; similar-looking paints can have different properties and should not be treated as interchangeable.

sections.title: Keep references together
paragraphs: Record the maker, finish, date and any manufacturer care notes visible on the original packaging. Retain only safe, appropriately stored samples.
Older coatings and disturbed surfaces can require specialist assessment. This is a record-keeping guide, not a stripping or sanding procedure.

sections.title: Review after changes
paragraphs: Update the record after redecoration, noting who completed the work and any new care requirements.
Avoid overwriting previous notes when an issue remains unresolved or the surface needs professional assessment.

articles.title: Furniture care records
articles.summary: Organise product care details and observations for frequently used furniture.

sections.title: Identify each item
paragraphs: Record the maker or model where known, the material described by its manufacturer and where assembly instructions are kept.
A fabric or timber appearance does not reliably establish cleaning compatibility or structural soundness.

sections.title: Check care information
paragraphs: Keep the maker's cleaning restrictions and load information available offline, with dated notes of wear or damage.
If a chair, table or shelf appears unstable, stop relying on it until suitable assessment or repair.

sections.title: Update the register
paragraphs: Note replacements, professional repairs and changes in location rather than deleting older observations.
Revisit the register when household needs or access arrangements change.

articles.title: External door seasonal observations
articles.summary: Record external door condition without attempting unsafe fire-door or lock modifications.

sections.title: Observe closure
paragraphs: From a safe position, note whether the door closes normally, draughts appear or the threshold shows visible damage.
Do not force a misaligned door or modify a fire-rated, security or communal door without permission and competent guidance.

sections.title: Track patterns
paragraphs: Record whether sticking or moisture marks coincide with particular weather and capture dated photographs if useful.
Keep photographs of locks and access points private; a visual check cannot establish security performance.

sections.title: Escalate concerns
paragraphs: Report persistent closure faults, damage or water ingress to the responsible property contact.
If the door forms part of an escape route, seek building-specific competent advice rather than a general DIY fix.

articles.title: Waste bin and recycling equipment log
articles.summary: Track waste containers and report defects without guessing local collection rules.

sections.title: List containers
paragraphs: Record indoor caddies and outdoor bins by location, condition and locally assigned waste stream.
Do not infer what is recyclable from bin colour alone; local collection requirements differ.

sections.title: Observe condition
paragraphs: Check visible lids, wheels and handles without lifting overloaded containers or reaching into unknown waste.
Record contamination or sharp hazards for the responsible collection or property service instead of handling them.

sections.title: Follow up
paragraphs: Log replacement requests, reference numbers and confirmed collection changes.
Keep equipment away from emergency exits and update the record when arrangements change.

articles.title: Tap and fixture identification records
articles.summary: Record visible household fixture details to support appropriate maintenance enquiries.

sections.title: Identify fixtures
paragraphs: Record each sink or basin location, visible manufacturer markings and any retained installation documentation.
Similar-looking taps can have incompatible internal components; do not guess hidden fittings from appearance.

sections.title: Document symptoms
paragraphs: Note dripping, stiffness or staining with dates and photographs without disassembling parts.
Active leakage near electrical equipment or uncertainty about isolation warrants appropriate professional assistance.

sections.title: Prepare an enquiry
paragraphs: Share the location, symptoms and verified model information with an authorised tradesperson or property manager.
After professional work, record any confirmed replacement part reference and care instructions.

articles.title: Household repair priority register
articles.summary: Track defects, contacts and outcomes without presenting an app's labels as a safety assessment.

sections.title: Capture observations
paragraphs: Record the location, date, observed symptoms and any photograph that can be shared safely.
Separate observed facts from speculation about causes and keep personal property information private.

sections.title: Route concerns
paragraphs: Flag immediate danger, essential-service loss, active water ingress and obstructed access for appropriate prompt escalation.
A generic priority label cannot determine statutory urgency or replace emergency services and competent advice.

sections.title: Confirm outcomes
paragraphs: Log who was contacted, the reference number and whether a visit resolved the problem.
Keep recurring issues visible rather than treating a scheduled appointment as completed maintenance.

articles.title: Curtain and blind condition records
articles.summary: Observe window covering condition and retain manufacturer safety information.

sections.title: Identify coverings
paragraphs: Record the type of curtain or blind at each window and where its manufacturer instructions can be found.
Different coverings have different cleaning and child-safety requirements; avoid generic product assumptions.

sections.title: Observe concerns
paragraphs: Note visible damage, jamming, loose-looking fittings or accessible cords from a safe position.
Do not climb onto furniture or alter child-safety devices without suitable instructions and competent help.

sections.title: Arrange follow-up
paragraphs: Record whether professional inspection, replacement or manufacturer advice is needed.
Where children may access cords or loops, seek current applicable safety guidance promptly.

articles.title: Private household key and access inventory
articles.summary: Organise authorised access information without publishing codes or key-cut details.

sections.title: List categories
paragraphs: Record which doors or facilities use keys or fobs without publishing access codes, key photographs or private addresses.
Store actual key locations and authorised holders only in an appropriately protected household record.

sections.title: Check availability
paragraphs: Confirm that authorised members know how to reach essential areas and identify missing credentials.
Do not copy restricted keys, bypass locks or alter shared access systems without permission.

sections.title: Review changes
paragraphs: Update holders and property-management contacts after moves, lost keys or changes in household membership.
A missing key with identifying information may require professional security advice rather than simply making a spare.
